Importing the data:

```{r}
library(e1071)
```

```{r}
train_data<-read.csv("../processed-data/football_train_data.csv")
test_data<-read.csv("../processed-data/football_test_data.csv")
```

**Pre-processing**

```{r}
# Pulling out the predictor variables from the outcome
predictors<-setdiff(names(train_data), "FTR")

selected_predictors <- predictors[
    colSums(is.na(train_data[, predictors, drop = FALSE])) == 0
]
```

That seems to be a problem - all predictors have at least one row with missing values

```{r}
which(is.na(train_data$AST))
train_data1<-train_data[-8808,]
```

I personally inspected this in the Excel file, it had N/A for almost all of the match statistics weirdly.
So removing it for now.
Trying again:

```{r}
sum(colSums(is.na(train_data1[, predictors, drop = FALSE])) == 0)
```

Only 10 - I would have thought 12; all the match statistics (non-betting odds)
Looking at which were fine:

```{r}
selected_predictors1 <- predictors[
    colSums(is.na(train_data1[, predictors, drop = FALSE])) == 0
]
selected_predictors1
```

AF and HF are the only two missing. Investigating:

```{r}
which(is.na(train_data$AF))
which(is.na(train_data$HF))
```

So now we'll use:

```{r}
train_data_NB<-train_data[-c(8808,32940,32949),]
selected_predictors_NB<- predictors[
    colSums(is.na(train_data_NB[, predictors, drop = FALSE])) == 0
]
```

which should work:

```{r}
sum(colSums(is.na(train_data_NB[, predictors, drop = FALSE])) == 0)
selected_predictors_NB
```






```{r}
nrow(train_data_NB)
nrow(test_data)
```
Now onto fitting an SVM:

```{r}
# Making outcome into a factor variable:

train_data_NB$FTR<-factor(train_data_NB$FTR, levels=c("H", "D", "A"))
test_data$FTR<-factor(test_data$FTR, levels=c("H", "D", "A"))

svm_model<-svm(FTR~., data=train_data_NB[, c("FTR", selected_predictors)],
               kernel="radial", cost=1, gamma=1/length(predictors), scale=TRUE)

```

```{r}
svm_predictions1<-predict(svm_model, newdata=test_data[, selected_predictors, drop=FALSE])

confusion_matrix_NB<-table(Actual=test_data$FTR, Predicted=svm_predictions1)
```

```{r}
confusion_matrix_NB
Accuracy<-mean(svm_predictions1==test_data$FTR)
Accuracy
```

So we have an accuracy of 57.5% which is quite bad. It didn't seem to predict many draws at all.
In fact we can do:

```{r}
round(diag(prop.table(confusion_matrix_NB, margin=1))*100, 2)
```

to see the percentage of correctly classified outcomes for each of Home Win, Draw and Away Win.
As we can see the model had a lot of trouble getting the draws, but seemed good at Home Wins and reasonable for
Away wins.

We will see how much of a difference knowing the bookmakers opening odds (specifically Bet365) can help it.
Setting up the dataset with the predictors:

```{r}
train_data_B<-train_data_NB[complete.cases(train_data_NB[, c("B365H", "B365D", "B365A")]),]
selected_predictors_B<-unique(c(selected_predictors, "B365H", "B365D", "B365A"))
```

and fitting the model:

```{r}
svm_model_B<-svm(FTR~., data=train_data_B[, c("FTR", selected_predictors_B)],
                 kernel="radial", cost=1, gamma=1/length(selected_predictors_B), scale=TRUE)
```

Now checking the performance:

```{r}
svm_predictions_B<-predict(svm_model_B, newdata=test_data[, selected_predictors_B, drop=FALSE])
confusion_matrix_B<-table(Actual=test_data$FTR, Predicted=svm_predictions_B)
```

```{r}
confusion_matrix_B
Accuracy_B<-mean(svm_predictions_B==test_data$FTR)
Accuracy_B
```
```{r}
round(diag(prop.table(confusion_matrix_B, margin=1))*100, 2)
```
This is a slight improvement for all outcomes.

```{r}
tuned_svm_NB<-readRDS("../MichaelM/best_svm_model_NB.rds")
tuned_svm_B<-readRDS("../MichaelM/best_svm_model_B.rds")

best_parameters_B<-tuned_svm_B$best_parameters_B

```

This is strange - K-fold CV is not giving much better performance.
Let's have a look at what the CV accuracy for each model was:

```{r}

tuned_svm_B$svm_tuning_B$best.performance
```
Wow - even though the test accuracy hasn't improved, it is actually better than the CV accuracy.
Let's test to see how it performs on the training data:

```{r}
train_predictions_B<-predict(best_svm_B, newdata=train_data_B[, selected_predictors_B, drop=FALSE])
train_confusion_matrix_B<-table(Actual=train_data_B$FTR, Predicted=train_predictions_B)

train_predictions_NB<-predict(best_svm_NB, newdata=train_data_NB[, selected_predictors_NB, drop=FALSE])
train_confusion_matrix_NB<-table(Actual=train_data_NB$FTR, Predicted=train_predictions_NB)
```

```{r}
train_accuracy_B<-sum(diag(train_confusion_matrix_B))/sum(train_confusion_matrix_B)
train_accuracy_NB<-sum(diag(train_confusion_matrix_NB))/sum(train_confusion_matrix_NB)

train_accuracy_NB
train_accuracy_B
```
The non-betting training data has pretty much the same accuracy for the training and test data, while the betting model seems to improve when using the test data.


**Investigating missingness for other variables**

```{r}
odds_var<-setdiff(names(train_data), selected_predictors_B)

missingness <- data.frame(
  Variable = odds_var,
  Missing_N = sapply(train_data[odds_var], function(x) sum(is.na(x))),
  Missing_Percent = sapply(
    train_data[odds_var],
    function(x) mean(is.na(x)) * 100
  )
)

missingness <- missingness[
  order(-missingness$Missing_Percent),
]
```

Checking the table:

```{r}
missingness
```

It seems that a few of the betting odds have relatively low missingness.
We will work with the 3 sites at under 12%
Imputing:

```{r}
library(mice)
```

```{r}
impute_vars <- c(
  "BWA", "BWD", "BWH",
  "WHA", "WHD", "WHH",
  "IWH", "IWD", "IWA"
)
```

```{r}
# Combining all of the predictors together: we are going to impute the missing values in the 12 rows total we had
# previously removed

selected_predictors_imputed <- unique(c(
  selected_predictors_B,
  impute_vars
))

train_imp <- train_data[
  , c("FTR", selected_predictors_imputed),
  drop = FALSE
]

```

```{r}
ini <- mice(
  train_imp,
  maxit = 0,
  printFlag = FALSE
)

meth <- ini$method
pred <- ini$predictorMatrix

meth["FTR"] <- ""

pred[, "FTR"] <- 0

for (v in selected_predictors_imputed) {
  if (anyNA(train_imp[[v]])) {
    meth[v] <- "pmm"
  } else {
    meth[v] <- ""
  }
}

imp <- mice(
  train_imp,
  method = meth,
  predictorMatrix = pred,
  m = 1,
  maxit = 5,
  seed = 123,
  printFlag = FALSE
)

train_imp_filled <- complete(imp, 1)

```

This should have imputed all of the values that were missing, let's check:

```{r}
colSums(is.na(train_imp_filled))
```

As this is good, we can once again try to build an svm model of this and we'll just check its baseline performance on the test set, but first we must check for missingness in the test set:

```{r}
colSums(is.na(test_data[, selected_predictors_imputed, drop=FALSE]))
sum(!complete.cases(test_data[, selected_predictors_imputed, drop = FALSE]))
```

Unfortunately unlike with the match statistics and Bet365 odds, there seems to be a fair amount of missingness - to be precise, (1436/8740)*100 = 16.43%. So a bit higher than the 12% cutoff from the training data, but as it's just for a baseline performance we will just impute the missing values in the test dataset as well.

```{r}
test_imp <- test_data[
  , selected_predictors_imputed,
  drop = FALSE
]

imp_test <- mice(
  test_imp,
  m = 1,
  method = "pmm",
  maxit = 5,
  seed = 123,
  printFlag = FALSE
)

test_imp_filled <- complete(imp_test, 1)
```

```{r}
# Checking that it's worked:
sum(is.na(test_imp_filled))
```

Time to fit the svm in the same way as the original models:

```{r}
# Converting result to factor again
train_imp_filled$FTR <- factor(
  train_imp_filled$FTR,
  levels = c("H", "D", "A")
)

svm_imputed <- svm(
  FTR ~ .,
  data = train_imp_filled[
    , c("FTR", selected_predictors_imputed),
    drop = FALSE
  ],
  kernel = "radial",
  cost = 1,
  gamma = 1 / length(selected_predictors_imputed),
  scale = TRUE
)
```

and test its performance:

```{r}
svm_predictions_imputed <- predict(svm_imputed, newdata = test_imp_filled)
confusion_matrix_imputed <- table(Actual = test_data$FTR, Predicted = svm_predictions_imputed)

Accuracy_imputed <- mean(svm_predictions_imputed == test_data$FTR)
```

```{r}
confusion_matrix_imputed
Accuracy_imputed
```

```{r}
round(prop.table(confusion_matrix_imputed, margin = 1) * 100,1)
```

Unfortunately as the accuracy is very slightly lower than with just the B365 odds, but still in turn reasonably higher than without any betting odds, we can reason that adding betting odds as a predictor improves predictive performance, but does not stack with more and more sites, i.e. there isn't any extra predictive power to be gleamed from multiple different sites in this experiment.

In particular, the SVM(s) had strong problems knowing when to classify a draw, though their marginal accuracy for away and especially home wins was relatively good. The accuracy reported on the test set actually ended up being higher than on the training data, so there is no evidence of over fitting. Earlier analysis of the data revealed that the lower leagues had a smaller proportion of home wins and a higher proportion of draws in comparison with the Premier League. Thus this is likely to have contributed to the increase in overall accuracy.


**Some graphs and plots**

```{r}
odds_vars <- c(
  "B365H", "B365D", "B365A",
  "BWA", "BWD", "BWH",
  "WHA", "WHD", "WHH",
  "IWH", "IWD", "IWA"
)

odds_data <- train_imp_filled[, odds_vars, drop = FALSE]

odds_correlations <- cor(
  odds_data,
  use = "pairwise.complete.obs"
)

heatmap_colours <- colorRampPalette(
  c("yellow", "orange", "red")
)(100)
```

```{r}
heatmap(
  odds_correlations,
  symm = TRUE,
  scale = "none",
  col = heatmap_colours,
  breaks = seq(-1, 1, length.out = 101),
  main = "Correlation Between Opening Odds"
)
legend("topright", legend=c("Negative (-1)", "Zero (0)", "Positive (+1)"),
         fill=c("yellow", "orange", "red"), cex=0.7, bty="n")


```

This is certainly evidence that many of the betting odds are highly correlated - in particular for the same outcomes across different sites. The red patches correspond to strong positive correlation - where the same results (Home, Draw, and Away) meet for different sites. Inversely the yellow patches are where Home win meets Away win. Meanwhile, the Draw odds seem more varied; they appear to be also highly positively correlated with the Away wins but more neutral when matched with the Home wins, which is interesting. 

These patterns suggest overlapping information between the bookmakers odds, though their individual usefulness for classification doesn't directly follow from just their correlations.
